subject: Post-demo: caching & pricing assumptions (Acme Health)
messages:
From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
To: Jamie Simmons <jamie.simmons@acmehealth.com>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 12 May 2026 14:03:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo: caching & pricing assumptions (Acme Health)

Jamie — thanks again for your time on the call today. Quick recap + next steps on the pricing/caching discussion we promised to follow up on.

Recap (high level)
- Use case: patient-facing summarization + templated response generation for care coordination. Short, repeatable prompts with variable patient fields.
- Primary cost levers: model selection, prompt/response token volumes, and prefix/prompt caching hit rate.
- Acme target: keep unit economics predictable; asked for target effective pricing in the ballpark of $/1M tokens (you mentioned wanting a target so you can benchmark).

Requested from you
- Estimated monthly token volumes (prompt vs response) or example traffic profile (calls/day, avg tokens per call).
- Target budget range (monthly) and target effective $/1M tokens you want us to aim for.

Caching assumptions we typically use in pricing conversations
- Prefix caching: we cache repeated prompt prefixes (templates, system prompts, common instructions). This only reduces billed prompt tokens (responses are generated fresh).
- Hit rate: percent of prompt tokens saved because a cached prefix is reused server-side. Typical ranges we see: 20% (low) / 40% (common) / 60%+ (high) depending on how templated the prompts are and whether keys are per-customer or shared across clients.
- TTL and scope: caching is customer-scoped by default with a short TTL (minutes) for dynamic templates; longer TTL possible for stable templates.

Simple worked example (to make the impact concrete)
- Assumptions: prompts = 100M tokens/month, responses = 300M tokens/month, base list price = $2.00 per 1M tokens (model-dependent; we’ll give a model-specific quote).
- Total raw tokens = 400M

Hit rate scenarios (prompt cache applies only to the 100M prompt tokens):
- 0% hit: billed tokens = 100M + 300M = 400M => cost = 400 * $2.00 = $800 => effective = $800 / 400M * 1M = $2.00 per 1M tokens
- 30% hit: billed prompts = 70M => billed tokens = 70M + 300M = 370M => cost = 370 * $2.00 = $740 => effective = $740 / 400M * 1M = $1.85 per 1M tokens
- 60% hit: billed prompts = 40M => billed tokens = 40M + 300M = 340M => cost = 340 * $2.00 = $680 => effective = $680 / 400M * 1M = $1.70 per 1M tokens

Key notes / caveats
- Caching impact depends heavily on where tokens live in the call (if prompts are short relative to responses, the percent savings on total token costs is smaller).
- Cold-starts and template churn reduce short-term hit rates — we recommend a short warm-up period for production traffic and instrumenting hit-rate metrics.
- For pricing contracts we typically show a banded estimate with conservative (20% hit) and optimistic (60% hit) scenarios.

Next steps
1) Jamie: please confirm the prompt vs response token split (or calls/day + avg tokens/call). If you have sample logs (even a CSV with counts) that’s perfect.
2) Vivek/Laura: can you generate a quick draft estimate (attach XLS) using the 3 hit-rate scenarios above and include peak concurrency notes? I attached the pricing template for the estimate.

Thanks — happy to jump on a short follow-up tomorrow to walk through the calc.

— Marcus

Thanks Marcus — this is really helpful. A few clarifications from our side: 

1) Ballpark volumes: we expect ~20M requests/month initially. Typical request = ~40 prompt tokens (template + fields) and ~120 response tokens. That maps to ~20M * (40+120) = 3.2B tokens/month total (prompt ~800M, response ~2.4B) — happy to share a CSV after we confirm the data export.
2) Budget: initial pilot budget is $15k/month, with the expectation of scaling after validation. Our procurement contact will need an exact quote.
3) Target effective $/1M: we’re aiming for <= $3.00 per 1M tokens effective across total tokens (after caching). Is that feasible?

Couple quick Qs: do your caching hit-rate examples assume prompt tokens are the only thing cached? Also — how does caching interact with privacy/regulatory requirements (per-customer cache vs shared)?

If we can get an estimate that shows pilot pricing under 30% and 60% hit assumptions that'd be super helpful for our forecasting.

— Jamie
Jamie Simmons
Head of Product, Acme Health
jamie.simmons@acmehealth.com

From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>

Cc: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Post-demo: caching & pricing assumptions (Acme Health)

Jamie — thanks, that volume profile helps a lot. I ran the numbers against the example in my prior note but swapped in your per-request tokens to make the math realistic for your traffic. Details below.

Assumptions (using your numbers)
- Requests/month: 20M
- Avg tokens per request: prompt = 40, response = 120
- Monthly prompt tokens = 20M * 40 = 800M
- Monthly response tokens = 20M * 120 = 2,400M (2.4B)
- Total raw tokens = 3,200M (3.2B)
- Base list price (example model) = $2.00 per 1M tokens (model choice can change this — we’ll include small/medium/large model price options in the formal estimate)

Billable tokens after cache (prompt cache only)
- 0% hit: billed = 800M + 2,400M = 3,200M => cost = 3,200 * $2.00 = $6,400 => effective = $6,400 / 3,200M * 1M = $2.00 per 1M
- 30% hit: billed prompts = 560M => billed = 560M + 2,400M = 2,960M => cost = 2,960 * $2.00 = $5,920 => effective = $5,920 / 3,200M * 1M = $1.85 per 1M
- 60% hit: billed prompts = 320M => billed = 320M + 2,400M = 2,720M => cost = 2,720 * $2.00 = $5,440 => effective = $5,440 / 3,200M * 1M = $1.70 per 1M

Interpretation vs your $15k/month pilot budget
- Under the $2.00/1M list price assumption and even with 0% caching, cost = ~$6.4k/month for 20M requests. That’s below your $15k pilot budget. 
- The bigger risk to budget is model choice (higher-capability models cost more per 1M tokens) and peak concurrency (affects latency/requirement for Dedicated capacity).

Privacy / cache scoping
- We scope caches per-customer by default (no cross-customer sharing). That meets most privacy/regulatory requirements. For PHI workloads we can additionally restrict TTL and keep the cache ephemeral; we’ll flag this in the formal estimate and include any KMS/HSM details required by procurement.

Next steps (clear asks)
- Jamie: if you can confirm model preference (or we can propose 2 model options: small/fast vs medium/quality), we’ll produce a formal estimate that includes the three hit-rate scenarios + model choices and peak concurrency notes.
- Vivek: can you produce the formal XLS estimate and include a short section on caching strategy (TTL, per-customer scoping, monitoring hooks) + recommended rollout (pilot -> scale)? I attached the template — feel free to reuse.

I’ll also include a short note to procurement with SOC2/attestation docs (Laura can you attach the SOC2 summary PDF in the formal quote please).

Happy to get on a quick call to walk through these numbers if helpful.

— Marcus
